videos.script: Colour on a sheet is a sentence. Most sheets say it badly. {{noise}} Here is every sale, with an arrow beside it. Eighty-six red arrows, pointing down. Nothing went down. The rule compared each sale with a range that a few big orders stretched. {{arrows}} Conditional formatting is a rule that decides how a cell looks from what it holds. Greater than a thousand. The ten largest. Above the average. {{rules}} The rule can be a formula, and then it can colour a whole row. One dollar sign decides whether it colours the right rows, one column, or everything. {{dollar}} It can shade a grid, too. Months down the side, channels across, and the busy months stand out at a glance. Or the grid can say only that wholesale is big, which you knew. {{heat}} Then the part that is not about Excel at all. What does the colour mean, and who can see it? Around one man in twelve has trouble telling red from green. So colour never says anything on its own. {{meaning}} By the end, every rule you keep says one thing, and says it to everybody who reads the sheet.
